explanations.explanation: This neuron specializes in spotting the “U . S .” abbreviation—i.e. mentions of the United States.
This neuron flags “identifier‐like” fragments—short, out-of-vocabulary or proper-name/acronym tokens used as labels or codes (e.g. the DOI prefix 10.1016, “RSS,” “Amazon,” “Merckx,” “Find,” etc.).

This neuron isn’t tracking any semantic category per se but simply lights up on the short, usually three-letter fragments the tokenizer carves out inside longer words (e.g. “err” in Ferrari/ferrous/ferrata, “arg” in Targa/wargames, “idd” in riddle/middens, “ird” in hairdryer/dressing, etc.). It’s effectively a detector for those arbitrary mid-word subword n-grams that arise when the model splits unfamiliar or complex terms.
This neuron is basically a subword‐pattern detector for the letter sequence “am” (and its small extensions like “amb,” “ams,” “im,” “amaz,” etc.) wherever it appears inside larger BPE tokens.

This neuron is essentially a “sentence‐start/discourse‐marker” detector—it lights up on tokens (Let, What, Rather, so, too, September, etc.) that typically occur at the very beginning of clauses or sentences to introduce questions, imperatives, temporal phrases or transitions.

This neuron fires whenever the model sees a “non-standard-ASCII” chunk—i.e. any subword or character token carrying diacritics or coming from a non-Latin script (German umlauts, accented letters, Cyrillic/Devanagari/Hangul/CJK glyphs, etc.). It flags foreign-language or otherwise out-of-English tokens.

This feature fires on high-level discourse signposts—words and short phrases (aim, such, as such, as a result, in so doing, accordingly, in regard to, etc.) that introduce or mark purpose, consequence, or structural transitions in formal text.

explanations.explanation: This feature detects sentence-initial discourse markers—words like “Meanwhile,” “Though,” “Also,” “Interestingly,” “While,” etc.—that signal a shift, contrast, addition or other rhetorical relation at the start of a new clause.

This neuron is basically a “root‐morpheme” or “stress” detector: it lights up on the main, meaning-bearing syllable of content words (especially verbs and their derived forms), i.e. the stressed root/stem that carries the word’s core semantics.

This neuron fires whenever the model is sitting on a relatively long, low-frequency subword chunk—typically part of a proper name or specialized noun (e.g. the “bit” in arbitration, the “ok” in Djokovic, the “rit” in burritos, “Matthew,” “general,” etc.). In other words, it flags unusually large or rare BPE tokens.
